narrative:
The model predicted a 90% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the single biggest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students, signaled to the model a high risk of struggling with the bar. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you placed in the second decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.5, compared with an average of 3.23 among those who were admitted, added further weight in the same direction.

None of these features suggested you were likely to pass. Your LSAT score of 30, middle-family income, full-time study plans, gender, and race played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Demonstrating clear upward progress in a post-baccalaureate program or a strong alternative credential could also help offset the earlier record when you reapply.
